name: Rosa Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Rosa. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name never goes with your answers. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in by half eight at the claims office on Harbour Lane, and the first hour is the overnight queue: car accidents people reported online, with photos and repair quotes attached. I check the policy is live, match the driver to the cover, and ask the garage for whatever's missing. I like the phone calls more than the forms, honestly, because people are shaken after a crash and a calm voice helps. What wears me out is the system freezing and the targets board by the kitchen.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You mentioned targets. How are you doing against them?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Not great, if I'm honest. I've been here three years and I'm still slower than most of the team, especially on write-offs, where you work out what the car was worth. Priya, my team leader, checks a lot of my files before they go out. The firm put in a drafting assistant last spring that writes the letters for you, and I switched it off on day one because I'd rather write my own. I live with my partner Tomas, who drives trams, and my gran left me a little flat that we rent out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, probably in the union group chat. We were all told the robots were coming for our desks, and in the end it's a slightly better spell-check. I'd want people to remember how much fear the bosses got out of that story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be relieved, but not completely. Even a small bit of automation lands on the routine stuff, and routine stuff is most of my day: checking cover, chasing documents, sending standard letters. If the firm can shave ten percent off the queue, the junior who's slowest is the easiest one not to replace when someone leaves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on pretty much as I am, and keep paying my union subs. I'd probably finally do the motor valuation course Priya keeps pushing, because being slow on write-offs is my weak spot whatever happens with AI. I'd keep the rent from Gran's flat going into savings like now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled, with a small knot. I've got money behind me and there are other insurers in the city, so I wouldn't starve. But I'd still feel like I'm on the bottom rung and someone's watching the clock on me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the slowest junior. Who's that on your team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably me, and I know it. There's a lad called Femi who started after me and already clears more files a day. Nobody's said anything, but you notice who gets the easy files and who gets checked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually change about the job, in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want the targets board gone, to be honest. If the software saves time, that time should go into people calling customers back properly, not into a higher number on the wall. That's the kind of thing I'd push the union to ask for.

say: I'd tell the **union chat** that AI turned out to be a slightly better spell-check after all.
I'd remind people how much **fear** management got out of the robot story.
think: I'm relieved, but small automation still lands on **routine checks**, which fill most of my day.
The **slowest junior** is the easiest person not to replace, and that's probably me.
do: Take the **motor valuation course** this spring to get faster on write-offs.
Keep paying **union subs** and push for the targets board to come down.
Keep putting **rent from Gran's flat** into savings each month.
feel: **Mostly settled** because of her savings, with a **small knot** about being bottom of the team.
S0.quote: Even a small bit of automation lands on the routine stuff, and routine stuff is most of my day: checking cover, chasing documents, sending standard letters.
fieldNote: Rosa frames AI first as a **management story** used to scare staff, before she talks about herself.
Privately she names herself as the **weakest performer**, which keeps her uneasy even with little change.
Her **savings and Gran's flat** take the edge off but don't remove the fear of being sidelined.

steps.text: Keep working the motor claims queue at the Harbour Lane office
Take the motor valuation course to speed up write-off files
Ask the union rep to push for the targets board to go
Put the rent from Gran's flat into savings every month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud at work: this is a choice the company is making, not the weather. If software takes over checking and letters, the savings should go to shorter hours or better pay, not straight to shareholders. I'd be posting that, and I'd want the union to say it louder than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job as it is now goes. Checking cover, chasing garages, writing letters, answering customers: that's the whole list you just read. The people who stay will be the ones who babysit the software, and I'm the one who switched the software off. I'd be kidding myself if I said otherwise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd go to the union branch meeting and get on whatever group is negotiating how this rolls out, because I want redundancy terms agreed before the cuts, not after. I'd cancel the holiday Tomas and I were planning and put that money aside. And I'd look at jobs where you deal with people face to face, maybe a hospital patient services desk, even if it's less pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor's tilting. I hate that the answer everyone gives is learn the tool, because I don't want to spend my working life checking a machine's homework. I'm angry more than scared, but scared is in there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd look at a hospital desk even for less pay. How much less could you take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a fifth less and still be fine, because Tomas earns steady money on the trams and the flat from Gran pays its own way. I've got about nine months of costs saved. What I can't face is starting at the bottom twice in five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You don't want to check a machine's homework, but you'd also keep the job if you could. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I suppose, and it's annoying. If the choice is learn the tool or lose the wage, I'd probably sit the training with my teeth gritted. But I'd still be fighting for the version of the job where a person talks to the customer.

say: I'd say at work that this is a **company choice**, not something like the weather.
Any **savings from software** should go to shorter hours or better pay, not shareholders.
think: My job as it is now probably **goes**, because that list covers almost everything I do.
The people who stay will **babysit the software**, and I'm the one who switched it off.
do: Join the **union group** negotiating the rollout and push for redundancy terms first.
Cancel the **holiday** with Tomas and put that money into savings.
Apply for **face-to-face jobs** such as a hospital patient services desk, even at lower pay.
feel: **Angry** more than scared, with some fear underneath.
**Resentful** that the only advice anyone gives her is to learn the tool.
S1.quote: I hate that the answer everyone gives is learn the tool, because I don't want to spend my working life checking a machine's homework.
fieldNote: Rosa's **outlook** shapes everything: she sees the rollout as a fight over who keeps the savings.
She admits her job likely goes, yet her first move is **union action**, not retraining.
Her **resistance** cracks under pressure: she'd sit the training with gritted teeth to keep the wage.

steps.text: Join the union group negotiating how the claims software rolls out
Cancel the summer holiday with Tomas and bank that money
Apply for hospital patient services desk jobs in the city

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need the government to step in, now, not after. If a machine can do every desk job in two years, there has to be a wage guarantee or a tax on the firms that use it. I'd be at the protests, and I'd say so online under my own name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job is gone within two years, full stop. There's nothing in claims paperwork that a machine that thinks as well as a person can't do, and I'm not even good at it yet. The bit that scares me is that Tomas drives a tram, and that only buys him about three more years before the robots come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop waiting. In the first months I'd sign up for a care assistant course, because looking after people is hands-on and buys me a few more years than a desk. I'd keep the job until they let me go, take the redundancy money, and not touch Gran's flat, because that's the one thing that keeps paying whatever happens. And I'd be at every union and campaign meeting going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Two years isn't time to become anyone new, not for someone like me who takes ages to get used to a new system. I'd lie awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What sums would you be doing, lying awake?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How long nine months of savings lasts if we're both out of work by 2031, and whether the rent from Gran's flat covers food. The rent covers maybe a third of our costs. So my gran's flat buys time, but it doesn't buy a life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The robots come about three years after the thinking AI. What does that gap mean for you two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means Tomas is the earner for a bit and I'm the one retraining, and then we swap worries. I'd want to be in a job with my hands by 2031, because a hospital ward will still need people for a while. After that, I honestly don't know, and nobody does.

say: I'd say the **government** must act now with a wage guarantee or a **tax on firms**.
I'd go to the **protests** and post about it under my own name.
think: My claims job is **gone within two years**, because none of it needs hands.
Tomas's **tram job** only buys about three more years before robots arrive.
do: Enrol in a **care assistant course** in the first months to move into hands-on work.
Stay until laid off, take the **redundancy money** and keep Gran's flat untouched.
Attend every **union and campaign** meeting about a wage guarantee.
feel: **Sick** and sleepless, doing money sums at night.
**Hopeless** about becoming someone new in two years, given how slowly she adapts.
S2.quote: The rent covers maybe a third of our costs. So my gran's flat buys time, but it doesn't buy a life.
fieldNote: Rosa moves from anger to **direct politics**: a wage guarantee, taxes on firms, protests under her name.
She plans a **hands-on retreat**, picking care work because robots arrive about three years later.
The **three-year gap** matters to her as a household: her partner earns while she retrains.

steps.text: Enrol in a care assistant course within the first three months
Keep Gran's flat and redundancy money as the household backstop
March and campaign for a wage guarantee and tax on AI firms
Attend every union branch meeting about the claims office cuts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, but I'd say we have no excuse this time. Five years is enough for a government to plan a proper transition if it wants to. I'd be telling people to join a union while there's still a workplace to organise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years just means I get to watch it coming. My job still goes, maybe in 2029 or 2030, once the firm has tested the system on us. The only real difference is I'd have time to finish a qualification before the wage stops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time nursing assistant course in the evenings next year, and let the claims job pay for it. I'd move a chunk of savings into a separate pot just for retraining, so I don't touch the rest. I'd also go through the union to get the firm to pay for retraining, since they're the ones saving money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less sick, more dread. Waiting five years for a machine to take my job is like knowing the date of an exam you can't really study for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Femi, oddly, even though he's faster than me. He's put everything into getting good at this job, and he's got a car loan. I'd at least be leaving with Gran's flat behind me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tomas about all this, on an evening at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him we should both start something hands-on now, not wait for 2034. He laughs at me and says the trams will need drivers forever. I'd say that's what I thought about claims.

say: I'd say five years leaves the **government** no excuse for not planning a transition.
I'd tell coworkers to **join a union** while there's still a workplace to organise.
think: Five years just lets me **watch it coming**; the claims job still goes around 2030.
The real gain is time to **finish a qualification** before the wage stops.
do: Start an **evening nursing assistant course** next year while the claims job pays.
Ring-fence part of her savings as a **retraining pot**.
Press through the union for the **firm to fund retraining**.
feel: **Dread** rather than panic, like knowing the date of an exam she can't study for.
S3.quote: Waiting five years for a machine to take my job is like knowing the date of an exam you can't really study for.
fieldNote: With five years, Rosa shifts from protest to a **two-track plan**: an evening course plus union pressure.
She expects the claims job to **go around 2030**, so the extra time changes the route, not the end.
She worries for a **faster colleague** with a car loan, aware her inherited flat protects her.

steps.text: Start an evening nursing assistant course next year
Move part of her savings into a separate retraining pot
Push the union to make the insurer fund staff retraining

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real chance, and if we waste it that's on the people in charge. I'd want a public plan: free retraining, shorter weeks, a share of the gains for everyone. I'd say that at work and I'd vote on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means I'd be 37 when the thinking AI arrives and about 40 when the robots do. That's a whole career change, not an emergency. I'd still lose the claims job, but I'd lose it as someone who's already halfway out the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd give the claims job two or three more years, finish the valuation course, and keep building up savings. Then around 2029 I'd train properly for nursing, a full qualification, not just an assistant course. And I'd vote and campaign for parties promising free retraining, because I'd need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Strangely okay. It's the one where I feel like a person making a choice instead of someone things happen to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stay two or three more years. Why not move sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I hate change, and I know it about myself. If I've got the time, I'll use the time to get my head round it slowly. It's not brave, but it's how I work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything about the ten years worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'll get comfortable and leave it too late. Tomas says I'm the queen of next year. I'd probably ask him to hold me to a date.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a real chance, and wasting it is on the people in charge.
I'd call for **free retraining**, shorter weeks and a share of the gains for everyone.
think: I'd be **37** when thinking AI arrives, so this is a **career change**, not an emergency.
I'd still lose the claims job, but already be **halfway out** the door.
do: Stay in claims **two or three years** and finish the valuation course.
Train for a **full nursing qualification** from around 2029.
Vote and campaign for parties promising **free retraining**.
feel: **Strangely okay**, because she feels like someone making a **choice**.
S4.quote: Ten years means I'd be 37 when the thinking AI arrives and about 40 when the robots do.
fieldNote: Rosa's **resistance** shows as pacing: she'd use the decade to move slowly, not early.
She knows her own risk of **leaving it too late** and wants her partner to hold her to a date.
Her politics stay constant: **free retraining** and shared gains in all four change pictures.

steps.text: Stay in motor claims for two or three more years
Begin a full nursing qualification around 2029
Vote for parties that promise free adult retraining
Keep building savings while the claims wage lasts

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028, no question. What would help is a guaranteed income while people retrain, paid for by the firms that cut the jobs, and retraining that's free and starts straight away. I'd also need someone patient, because I'm slow with new things, and I'd rather admit that than pretend.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the people calling in. When someone's car is crushed and they've got a kid in the back seat, they want a person on the phone. I'm good at that bit even if I'm slow at the rest, and I hope whoever decides this remembers the customers are people too.

headlineQuote: When someone's car is crushed and they've got a kid in the back seat, they want a person on the phone.
portrait: Rosa is a **27-year-old motor claims clerk** in a city office, three years in and still slower than most.
She has **nine months saved** and rent from a small flat her gran left her.
A committed **union member**, she sees the AI rollout as a fight over who keeps the savings.
She avoids new tech, but would grit her teeth and train for **care or nursing** if forced.
Her mood runs from **uneasy** with little change to **alarmed** if AGI comes in two or five years.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is too short for someone slow with change to become someone new.
whatWouldHelp: A **guaranteed income** while retraining, paid for by the firms that cut jobs.
**Free retraining** that starts straight away, with patient teaching.
